strengths: The task is practically motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed appearance addresses a limitation of image-only and text-only retrieval. ITCPR provides a useful initial benchmark with 2,202 queries, 20,510 gallery images, and three source datasets.

The two-stage framework is simple and computationally practical. It uses existing person image–caption data without composed-retrieval training triplets, and freezing the encoders during textual-inversion training reduces training cost.

The improvements over feature averaging with the same fine-tuned encoders are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Rank-1 increases from 32.02% to 45.55%, and mAP from 41.83% to 55.26%. These comparisons support the usefulness of the composition mechanism.

The paper includes substantial ablations covering supervision, training-data quantity and quality, network architecture, and fusion. The supplementary timing measurements and implementation settings are helpful, and the limitation concerning explicit identity preservation is honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The main comparison with Pic2Word is compromised by an encoder–mapper mismatch: Table 1 explicitly states that its mapper was trained with original CLIP parameters but is also evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This does not establish superiority over a properly adapted competitor. Table 2 provides useful, more controlled ITC ablations, but these show smaller gains; matched comparisons on ViT-L/14 and against the cited textual-inversion method [2] remain necessary.

The methodological novelty is limited. Mapping image features into a pseudo-word for composition closely follows Pic2Word, while the encoder fine-tuning and matching losses reuse established person-retrieval techniques. The benchmark and alternative supervision are useful contributions, but the paper does not clearly establish a substantial technical advance beyond their combination.

Model selection is insufficiently separated from evaluation. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet Appendices C.3–C.5 select optimal architectures and fusion configurations using its results. No independent selection protocol or untouched final evaluation is described. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates further limit conclusions about the smaller ablation and ensemble improvements.

The benchmark requires stronger validation and documentation. Pooled results obscure differences among its three sources and types of appearance change, and clothing-invariant person-retrieval baselines are absent. Annotation agreement, detailed distractor selection, and the coverage of the nearest-neighbor false-negative audit are not reported, making relevance-label completeness and benchmark reproducibility difficult to assess.

There is a concrete ambiguity in the training objective: Equation (1) divides one-hot masked-token cross-entropy by both the number of masked tokens and vocabulary size. Under the unweighted sum in Equation (5), this would greatly suppress the implicit-relation loss. The manuscript should clarify whether this normalization is implemented or is a typographical error.

Despite explicitly motivating surveillance and public-security applications and proposing a dataset release, the paper lacks substantive discussion of privacy, dataset reuse permissions, misidentification harms, and potential misuse. These omissions warrant attention alongside the experimental concerns.
